Code-first course: every lab solves one Acme business problem, with pinned library versions. Analogy: the base model is a new hire that everyone can rent. Weights = training the hire (habits, format, judgment). Context = handing them the current policy binder with each question. The data loop = the QA team that keeps the training material and the exam honest. Click 0: one base model, the same for everyone. Your data is the only thing you own. Click 1, weights. SFT (supervised fine-tuning) = train on example input and answer pairs. LoRA = train small adapter matrices instead of all weights. GRPO = sample a group of answers, score each one with a reward function, and push toward the better ones. DPO (direct preference optimization) = learn from chosen versus rejected pairs; it uses no reward function. Labs 1–2 are SFT, Labs 3–4 are GRPO rewards, Lab 5 is DPO. Click 2, context. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) = retrieve documents into the prompt at query time; the weights do not change. Rule: facts that change go to context; behaviour, format and decisions go to weights. Lab 9 builds and checks the eval set for the HR policy RAG assistant. Click 3, the data loop that feeds all three: contract = schema checks on each incoming row (Lab 6, the start of the loop); label = humans add answers (Lab 6); synthesize, dedup, verify = generate new examples, remove near-duplicates and test leaks, reject wrong items (Lab 9); eval = score on held-out cases (Lab 10); drift = watch production data change, which starts the next round (Labs 7–8). Likely question: "Do I need to train at all?" Not always. Chapter 01 shows how to decide before you spend GPU hours.

Shopify Building production-ready agentic systems
Each team built its reward or eval signal from its own data first. That signal is the part you cannot rent.
This slide is the reason for the course: three teams that rent or reuse base models, and win with their own data, rewards and evals. Click 1, Cursor (rewards lever): real-time RL for Composer. They serve a checkpoint, turn user interactions into rewards (did the edit stay in the codebase, did the user send an unhappy follow-up), update the weights, pass an eval gate on CursorBench, and deploy. One cycle takes about five hours. The A/B test gave 3.13% fewer dissatisfied follow-ups and 10.3% lower latency. Click 2, Databricks KARL (data loop plus RL): an agent synthesizes grounded question-answer pairs, a dedup agent removes overlap with the eval set, solver agents drop questions that are always or never solved, a quality filter removes bad items, then off-policy RL trains GLM 4.5 Air. With 10 parallel rollouts (test-time compute) KARL scores 67.5 on KARLBench, the same as Claude 4.6 Opus; the base model scores 52.6. Source: the KARL tech report, Table 4. Click 3, Shopify Sidekick (eval lever): Cohen's kappa measures agreement beyond chance; 1.0 is perfect, 0 is chance. They tuned the judge until kappa went from 0.02 to 0.61, against 0.69 between two humans, and only then trained with GRPO and gated rewards. Analogy: three restaurants with the same supplier; the menu is different because each one tastes and scores its own dishes. Likely question: "Do these numbers transfer to my team?" No. They show what to measure. Your own eval set decides.

Analogy: think of the course as a consulting engagement. Acme has four client teams and ten tickets; each lab closes one ticket for one team. Click 0: the rule for the course order. Chapter 01 has no lab, because it decides which lever to use (weights, context or data, from the hero slide). So Lab N runs in Chapter N + 1: Lab 4 is in Chapter 05. Click 1, Labs 1–2, SFT: the refunds assistant learns answer format from 2,992 real refund chats (the Bitext customer-support dataset, REFUND rows); the claims extractor turns claim text into JSON with 4-bit QLoRA on Qwen3-4B. A T4 runs both if you set fp16 (a T4 has no bf16). Click 2, Labs 3–5, rewards and preferences: Lab 3 writes reward functions and unit-tests them on a CPU; its last two steps send the same reward to the OpenAI grader API and to Vertex AI, so they need keys. Lab 4 trains GRPO on claim payouts with an exact-answer reward. Lab 5 trains DPO on chosen versus rejected support replies. Click 3, Labs 6–8, data quality on a CPU: Lab 6 writes a schema contract for claims intake; experts can label only 100 claims a day, so the model picks which rows go to them. Lab 7 checks drift and leakage, then sets the fraud alert threshold from costs: a missed fraud costs $120, a wrongly held refund costs $15. Lab 8 finds drift and wrong labels in ticket triage and sends unsure tickets to a human. Click 4, Labs 9–10, synthetic data and eval: Lab 9 generates HR policy test questions, then dedups and verifies them and checks the LLM judge. Lab 10 builds the release quality card: pass rate per slice with confidence intervals, used as a CI gate. Likely question: "Must I do the labs in order?" No. Each lab has its own data; the order only follows the course.

Choose the lever

Facts → context. Behaviour → weights. Eval decides.

This chapter makes one decision before anyone rents a GPU: which lever fixes which failure. Press through the diagram. The Acme refunds assistant gives a wrong answer, and the first step is not a fix: it is an eval of 20 or more real cases, with each failure tagged. A missing fact, such as "14-day window" when the policy says 30 days, is a knowledge failure, so it goes to context and RAG (retrieval-augmented generation). A missing refund_amount field is a behaviour failure, so it goes to SFT (supervised fine-tuning on example answers) or RL (reinforcement learning against a reward score). After each fix you re-run the same eval. Analogy: a new support agent who does not know the refund policy needs the handbook; one who knows the policy but writes messy replies needs coaching. Likely student question: "Can one fine-tune fix both?" It can try, but slide 6 shows that SFT on new facts raises hallucination, so facts stay in retrieval. Next: the ladder shows the order in which to try the levers.

Climb the ladder one rung at a time; the eval decides each step

Prompt only: 41%. Facts and format both fail.
Long context: 52%. The Acme KB is over ~200k tokens, so some facts still miss.
RAG: 63%. Retrieval finds the policy. Facts pass; format still fails.
SFT (LoRA): 85%. Training on example answers fixes the format.
DPO and RL stay closed: no preference pairs and no trusted reward yet.

Knowledge → RAG.
Behaviour → tuning.

Docs OpenAI: Optimizing LLM accuracy
Read the ladder bottom-up: each rung needs more data and more time than the one below, so you climb only when the eval says the current rung is not enough. The Acme refunds assistant starts at prompt only and passes 41% of the refund eval; all gauge numbers are illustrative. Long context helps a little, but the Acme knowledge base is bigger than about 200k tokens, so we move to RAG, which fixes the fact half. SFT with LoRA (low-rank adapters, a cheap way to fine-tune) fixes the format half. DPO (direct preference optimization: train on chosen versus rejected answers) and RL or RFT (reinforcement fine-tuning against a grader) stay closed until you have preference pairs or a reward you trust. Analogy, as on the chapter slide: the handbook fixes missing facts, coaching fixes behaviour. One real number: in OpenAI's Icelandic grammar case, adding RAG to a fine-tuned GPT-4 dropped BLEU (overlap with reference text, higher is better) from 87 to 83, because the task was behaviour and the retrieved text added noise. Likely student question: "Why not skip to RL?" RL needs at least one correct sampled answer per prompt to learn anything; the probe slide at the end of this chapter shows how to check. Databricks Frontier data agent Google Cloud Top five tuning use cases
Databricks measured Genie Code on 401 internal data tasks with a 20-minute budget and an independent judge; the numbers are vendor-reported. First click: accuracy, 76.6% for Genie Code against 72.1% for the best general coding agent. Second click: cost, $0.55 against $1.09 per task. Genie Code also used 8.3 tool calls per task, the fewest of any agent tested, and Databricks says "accuracy and cost did not trade off". The gain came from context: semantic search over the catalog and a persistent memory of tables, with the model weights unchanged. Compare it to a new support hire: give them the policy binder before you send them on a training course. The counter-case is NextNet on Google Cloud: its failure was behaviour and cost, so tuning Gemini Flash won with +80% accuracy, −90% cost and −60% latency, partly because the prompt template shrank from 2,000 to 200 tokens. A likely question is "so when do I tune?": tune when the failure is behaviour, format, cost or latency. For Acme, the missing refund facts are a context fix: a search tool over the policy documents plus session memory. Next: a new paper shows why facts trained into weights backfire.
arXiv Aug 2026 · knowledge-aligned SFT

SFT on facts the base lacks raises hallucination: filter or retrieve

arXiv:2608.30987 31 Aug 2026

Stick to What You Know: Knowledge-Aligned SFT

Targets with facts the base lacks drive hallucination. Recall Rewrite keeps only recalled claims and cuts it (Qwen3 4B, OLMo 3 7B).
Acme: put refund-policy numbers in RAG. Use SFT for format and tone.
If you must internalize facts · arXiv 2607.21861
Documents baked into a LoRA adapter, closed-book QA:
raw targets
57.7%
curated answers
85.7%
Curate the targets first.
arXiv 2608.30987 arXiv 2607.21861
Start with the Acme failure: the refunds assistant gives wrong policy numbers, and the reflex is to fine-tune them in. Read the left side as the method of the August paper. One SFT target answer holds 10 claims. A probe asks the base model about each claim 8 times; a claim is kept only if at least 5 of the 8 probes recall it, and the target is rewritten without the dropped claims. The first paper shows that SFT targets with facts the base does not know drive hallucination, and Recall Rewrite reduced factual hallucination on the WildHalu and Biography tests. The dots and the bar are an illustration of the method, not the paper's data. Think of SFT as teaching a style of answering, not as filling a library: the library is retrieval. The honest counterpoint is the July paper: if you must bake documents into a LoRA adapter, curation into short canonical answers moved closed-book accuracy from 57.7% to 85.7%. A third paper, SFT-as-Context (arXiv 2610.11132), is about keeping general skills after SFT; we cover it in the SFT chapter on forgetting. A likely question is "how much does hallucination drop?": the paper reports the reduction per benchmark; read the tables before you quote a single number. Cursor real-time RL Vercel v0 models Chroma Context-1 Ramp via Prime Intellect Intercom via VentureBeat
Five production teams, one shape. Inside your harness a router sends each request either to a swappable frontier model or to a specialist that the team trained for one workflow. The specialists are peers of the frontier model, not copies trained from it: Chroma started from gpt-oss-20b, Ramp from a 35B model, Intercom from an undisclosed open-weights base. Cursor runs a five-hour RL loop on live traffic; Vercel trained a fixer that writes 8,130 characters per second against 559 for gemini-2.5-flash; Chroma and Ramp trained retrieval and search subagents. Intercom is the large case: hundreds of billions of parameters, still for one workflow, and its number is vendor-reported. Vercel is from June 2025; the other four are from 2026. Think of a hospital: the general physician stays, and you add a specialist clinic for the case you see every day. A likely question: "what is the router in my ADK app?" It is plain code or a small classifier that picks the model per request. Another: "why not fine-tune the frontier model itself?" Speed, cost and portability: the base keeps improving, while your specialist, data and evals stay yours. For Acme, the specialist is the refunds assistant, trained only for the format failure. refunds/grade.py · no SDK import
import json, re
def grade(sample, item) -> float:
    m = re.search(r"\{.*?\}", sample["output_text"], re.DOTALL)
    try:
        out = json.loads(m.group(0)) if m else None
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        out = None
    if not isinstance(out, dict):
        return 0.0
    if out.get("decision") != item["gold_decision"]:
        return 0.0
    try:
        amt = float(out["refund_amount"])
        ok = abs(amt - float(item["gold_amount"])) <= 0.01
    except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError):
        ok = False
    return 1.0 if ok else 0.5
Parse defensively. No JSON, bad JSON or a JSON list gives 0.0. The grader never raises.
Gold labels come from the dataset row (item), not from a vendor API.
Smooth score: 1.0 right amount, 0.5 right decision only, 0.0 wrong.
expected · item = approve, 49.99
{"decision":"approve","refund_amount":49.99}  -> 1.0
{"decision":"approve","refund_amount":40}     -> 0.5
Sure! I approved it.                          -> 0.0

OpenAI deprecations Vertex Gemini RFT Fireworks RFT
Tell the problem first. OpenAI is winding down self-serve fine-tuning: organizations that never fine-tuned lost job creation on 7 May 2026, organizations with no fine-tuned inference in the last 60 days lost it on 2 July 2026, and active customers can create new jobs only until 6 January 2027. RFT ran on o4-mini, and the ft-o4-mini snapshot shut down on 23 October 2026, so OpenAI RFT has already ended. Vertex Gemini RFT is Pre-GA and not for production or confidential data, and Fireworks managed RFT takes no new jobs. Recap the three dates on the tiles before the next click. The lesson is like moving house: the furniture is your training data, your grader and your eval set, and the vendor is only the truck. The grade function has no SDK import, so the same logic runs behind a TRL reward function, a Vertex code reward or a Bedrock Lambda reward, with a thin adapter for each. A likely question: "is the score scale the same everywhere?" Not quite: Vertex clips rewards to the range -1 to 1, so the Vertex adapter maps 0..1 to -1..1 with 2 * score - 1; chapter 4 shows the full adapters. Next: eight checks that turn this chapter into a decision.
Best practices

Eight checks pick the lever before any GPU hour

1 · Eval
  • Build 20-50 eval cases from real failures.Tag each: knowledge or behaviour.
2 · Context
  • Fix knowledge failures with context or RAG first.Genie Code: +4.5 pts at half the cost.
3 · RL gating
  • Check pass@k > 0 before RL.pass@k: 1+ of k samples correct. Then validate RFT on 100-200 examples.
  • Screen base models before you pay for RL.A cheap test predicts the post-RL SWE-bench rank.
  • Distill on-policy when a strong teacher exists.AIME'24: 74.4% at 1,800 GPU-h; RL 67.6% at 17,920.
Do not
  • Do not SFT new facts unless you curate them.Hallucination rises; prefer retrieval.
  • Do not start RFT above 95% reward.Bedrock: RFT "might be unnecessary".
  • Do not lock data to one vendor.Keep JSONL, graders and evals portable.
Anthropic Demystifying evals AWS Nova RFT Docs Bedrock RFT Thinking Machines On-policy distillation arXiv 2610.10478 arXiv 2608.30987
These eight checks run before anyone books a GPU, in the same order as the chapter. Eval: start with 20 to 50 eval cases from real Acme refund failures, and tag each failure as knowledge or behaviour. Context: the missing policy facts go to context or RAG, as Databricks Genie Code did to gain 4.5 points at half the cost. RL gating: AWS says RFT requires that the model can produce at least one correct solution among several attempts; that is pass@k greater than zero, where pass@k means at least one of k sampled answers is correct. AWS also suggests a small validation run of 100 to 200 examples before a full RFT job. A base-model screen (arXiv 2610.10478) predicts which base will rank best on SWE-bench after RL, so you choose the base first. On-policy distillation means the student samples and the teacher grades every token; Thinking Machines reached 74.4% on AIME'24 with 1,800 GPU-hours, against 67.6% and 17,920 GPU-hours for RL. The don'ts: do not SFT new facts unless you curate them, do not start RFT when reward is already above 95% because Bedrock says it might be unnecessary, and do not lock your data to one vendor. Think of it as a doctor's triage: you do not operate before you read the chart. A likely question: "how do I check pass@k in practice?" The next slide runs that probe on the Acme base model.
Build · Acme refunds · base-model probe

Probe the base model 8 times per prompt before you pay for RL

cd refunds && python probe.pyopenai==3.37.0vllm==0.31.0 server
refunds/probe.py
import json
from openai import OpenAI      # any OpenAI-compatible server, e.g. vLLM
from grade import grade        # refunds/grade.py, the portable grader

client, MODEL = OpenAI(), "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507"
rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("eval_set.jsonl")]   # 20-50 prompts
passes = solved = 0
for row in rows:
    r = client.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, messages=row["messages"],
                                       temperature=1.0, n=8)
    s = [grade({"output_text": c.message.content}, row) for c in r.choices]
    passes += sum(x == 1.0 for x in s)
    solved += any(x == 1.0 for x in s)
print(f"pass rate {passes / (8 * len(rows)):.2f}")
print(f"pass@8 > 0 on {solved}/{len(rows)} prompts")
output · illustrative, 4 prompts shown
pass rate 0.41
pass@8 > 0 on 4/4 prompts   # not 0, not > 95%: RFT is in range
Probe the base model8 samples per prompt, temperature 1.0
always 0SFT firstno RL signal
> 95%Stopship the prompt
otherwiseRFTGRPO: RL on sample groups
you are here
This is check 3 as code. The probe samples the Acme base model 8 times per eval prompt at temperature 1.0, scores every sample with the same grade() function we keep portable, and counts two numbers. The pass rate is the share of samples that score a full 1.0; pass@8 greater than zero means at least one of the 8 samples is fully correct for that prompt. The tree is the decision. If the reward is always 0, RL has no signal: do SFT first. If the reward is already above 95%, Bedrock says RFT might be unnecessary: ship the prompt. Otherwise RFT is in range; GRPO, the usual RFT algorithm, compares the samples in a group, so it needs some passes and some fails. On the right, 4 of the 20 to 50 eval prompts are shown; the dots are illustrative: 13 of 32 samples pass, so the pass rate is 0.41, and every prompt has at least one pass. Analogy: a coach tests whether the athlete can do the move at least sometimes before planning drills. Likely question: "why temperature 1.0?" With low temperature all 8 samples are the same answer, so the probe and GRPO both see no variety. Next: chapter 2 takes the format failure to SFT with TRL and LoRA in Lab 1.
Chapter 02

SFT with TRL and LoRA

Train only on assistant tokens, train all linear layers, and prove the merge kept behaviour. Step 1 runs on a CPU; steps 2–5 need one GPU.

Qwen3-0.6B + LoRA r=16 trl 1.16.0 Docs TRL SFT Trainer
This chapter builds one thing end to end: the Acme refunds assistant. We take the 2,992 REFUND rows of the Bitext customer-support dataset (split into train and eval later), train Qwen3-0.6B with LoRA, merge it, prove the merge kept behaviour, and serve it. Watch the loop: the grey user tokens get label -100, which is PyTorch's ignore_index, so cross-entropy skips them; only the coral assistant tokens are in the loss. That gradient updates only the small B and A matrices, so the new weight is W plus B times A, and the base W stays frozen. The 1.67% is for rank 16 on all linear layers; other settings give other numbers. Analogy: the base model is a printed textbook, and LoRA is a thin set of sticky notes you can peel off or print in. Likely question: "Why not train the user tokens too?" Because then the model learns to write customer complaints, not refund answers. After the open-weights path we use the same data on managed Gemini tuning and on Gemma 4 with Unsloth. Next: Lab 1 starts on a laptop CPU, by printing the loss mask before any GPU time.
Lab 1 Acme refunds assistant · step 1 of 5

Look before you train: print exactly which tokens SFT learns from

refunds_sft/step1_inspect_mask.py · trl 1.16.0 · transformers 5.20.2
# step1_inspect_mask.py - which tokens does SFT learn from? (CPU)
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from trl import get_training_chat_template
from common import SYSTEM   # refunds system prompt, shared by all steps
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B")
# {{Order Number}} is literal Bitext text: the model must copy it
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
  {"role": "user", "content": "Where is my refund for {{Order Number}}?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "I'm sorry for the wait. Let me check."},
  {"role": "user", "content": "Thanks. Can you check it now?"},
  {"role": "assistant", "content": "{{Order Number}}: it is on its way."}]
tpl = get_training_chat_template(tok) or tok.chat_template  # None: OK
orig = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False)
print("orig == patched:", orig == tok.apply_chat_template(
    messages, tokenize=False, chat_template=tpl))
out = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, chat_template=tpl, tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True, return_assistant_tokens_mask=True)
mask = out["assistant_masks"]       # 1 = in the loss, 0 = label -100
print(f"tokens={len(mask)} trained={sum(mask)}")
print(repr(tok.decode([t for t, m in zip(out["input_ids"], mask) if m])))
assert sum(mask) > 0, "no assistant tokens in the loss"   # run this in CI

Stock Qwen3 drops the earlier <think> block from history. TRL's template keeps it, so every turn trains the same way.
Mask 1 = trained. The trainer gives 0 positions label -100 (ignore_index).
<|im_end|> is trained, so the model learns to stop.
Train with an empty <think></think> → serve with enable_thinking=False: the same prefix, in steps 4 and 5.
Before we spend any GPU time, we print what SFT will actually learn from. This script runs on a laptop CPU in seconds. Step 1: TRL swaps the stock Qwen3 chat template for its training template, because the stock one drops the think block from earlier assistant turns, so history renders differently from the final turn; if TRL returns None, the template is already training-ready and we keep it. Step 2: the assistant mask is what assistant_only_loss turns into labels: a 0 becomes label -100, which cross-entropy ignores, so only the coral tokens are in the loss. Step 3: the end-of-turn token must be inside the trained span, or the model never learns to stop; the assert is the line to copy into CI. Analogy: it is a highlighter over the transcript, and the model only studies the highlighted lines. The counts are illustrative and depend on the tokenizer version. The rule to remember: we train with an empty think block, so every inference call in steps 4 and 5 must pass enable_thinking=False, which prefills the same block. Likely question: "What about Gemma 4?" TRL 1.16 does not patch its template and raises a ValueError; we fix that with Unsloth later in this chapter. Next: step 2 turns this mask into one SFTConfig with assistant_only_loss=True.
Lab 1 Acme refunds assistant · step 2 of 5

One SFTConfig: assistant-only loss, BFD packing, bf16, all-linear LoRA

step2_train.py · trl 1.16.0 · peft 0.21.2 · train(): step 3
import torch
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer
from common import refund_splits  # Bitext rows, category == "REFUND"
# 2,992 rows: get_refund · track_refund · check_refund_policy
ds = refund_splits()                # messages, random 95/5 split
args = SFTConfig(output_dir="qwen3-0.6b-refund-lora",
    model_init_kwargs={"dtype": torch.bfloat16,     # else float32
        "attn_implementation": "kernels-community/flash-attn2"},
    assistant_only_loss=True, max_length=1024,
    packing=True, packing_strategy="bfd",           # padding-free
    per_device_train_batch_size=8, gradient_accumulation_steps=2,
    learning_rate=2e-4, num_train_epochs=2,
    warmup_steps=0.03,                              # float = ratio
    eval_strategy="epoch", save_strategy="epoch",   # keep every ckpt:
    load_best_model_at_end=False,                   # pick by task metric
    logging_steps=10, report_to="none", seed=42)
peft_config = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM")
trainer = SFTTrainer(model="Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", args=args,
    train_dataset=ds["train"], eval_dataset=ds["test"],
    peft_config=peft_config)
trainer.model.print_trainable_parameters()
refund_splits() is a random 95/5 split, so paraphrases leak into eval. Also score a held-out set of new phrasings.

output · illustrative
trainable params: 10,092,544 || all params: 606,142,464 || trainable%: 1.6650
This is the whole training call for the Acme refunds assistant: the 2,992 Bitext REFUND rows over three intents, Qwen3-0.6B and one LoRA config. The data helper in common.py filters category REFUND, maps each row to system, user and assistant messages, and makes a random 95/5 split. Walk the four bands. One: set dtype to bf16, because TRL loads a string model id in float32, which doubles the weight memory. Two: assistant-only loss plus BFD packing switches on padding-free batches, which need FlashAttention, so we load the kernels-community flash-attn2 kernel; that needs an Ampere or newer GPU such as an L4 or A10G. Three: a learning rate of 2e-4, about ten times the full fine-tuning default of 2e-5, and a float warmup_steps below 1 is a ratio. Four: target_modules all-linear; without it PEFT trains only q_proj and v_proj, 2,293,760 parameters instead of 10,092,544. We save one checkpoint per epoch and do not load the best one by eval_loss, because the last slide of this chapter picks the checkpoint by generated output. Think of LoRA targets like the gears you allow a mechanic to adjust: give access to two and the car still drives, but not well. A likely question: "Is a random split enough?" No: Bitext has many paraphrases of each request, so a random split puts near-copies on both sides; keep a separate set of new phrasings for the final check. Run the script and keep the log with tee. The numbers here are illustrative and the runtime depends on your GPU, but the keys are real: TRL logs entropy, mean_token_accuracy and num_tokens next to the loss. Token accuracy is teacher-forced: the model sees the gold prefix and we check only the next token, so it is not the same as a generated answer. Click 2: with eval_strategy epoch we get one eval per epoch, and eval_packing follows packing, so eval loss uses the same token layout as training; set eval_packing=False if you want per-example numbers. Loss falls from 1.912 and token accuracy rises to about 0.85. Click 3: save_model writes only the adapter: 10.1 million parameters times 4 bytes, because PEFT keeps adapter weights in fp32, so about 40 MB next to a 1.2 GB bf16 base. Think of the adapter as a patch file, not a new program. A likely question: "Can I ship the checkpoint with the lowest eval_loss?" Answer: no, choose on a generated task metric, as the last slide of this chapter shows. Next: step 4 merges this adapter into the base and proves the merge kept behaviour.
Lab 1 Acme refunds assistant · step 4 of 5

Merge the adapter, then assert the argmax did not change

refunds_sft/step4_merge_and_verify.py · peft 0.21.2 · transformers 5.20.2
import torch
from peft import PeftModel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from common import refund_splits
BASE, ADAPTER = "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", "qwen3-0.6b-refund-lora/final"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE)
# Merge into a bf16 (16-bit) base, never a 4-bit base.
base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
peft_model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, ADAPTER).eval()
test = refund_splits()["test"].select(range(20))   # 20 held-out rows
encs = [tok.apply_chat_template(r["messages"][:2],   # SYSTEM + user
            add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False,
            return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True) for r in test]
with torch.no_grad():
    ref = [peft_model(**e).logits.float() for e in encs]
merged = peft_model.merge_and_unload(safe_merge=True)  # returns the model
with torch.no_grad():
    new = [merged(**e).logits.float() for e in encs]
diff = max((a - b).abs().max().item() for a, b in zip(ref, new))
same = all(torch.equal(a.argmax(-1), b.argmax(-1)) for a, b in zip(ref, new))
print(f"max |logit diff| = {diff:.4f}  same argmax, 20 prompts: {same}")
assert same, "merge changed the argmax - do not ship"
merged.save_pretrained("qwen3-0.6b-refund-merged")  # ~1.2 GB, no peft
tok.save_pretrained("qwen3-0.6b-refund-merged")
python step4_merge_and_verify.py
Load the base in bf16. A 4-bit base re-rounds the merged weights.
Merge the PeftModel and keep the returned model. safe_merge=True stops on NaNs.
bf16 re-rounds W + B·A·α/r (α=32, r=16). 0.0625 is one bf16 step near logit 10. The argmax must not move.
output · illustrative
max |logit diff| = 0.0625  same argmax, 20 prompts: True
This is step 4 of the refunds lab: we fold the 40 MB adapter into the bf16 base and prove that behaviour did not change. Load the base in bf16, because merging into 4-bit bitsandbytes layers re-quantizes, and PEFT warns: "Merge lora module to 4-bit linear may get different generations due to rounding errors." Call merge_and_unload on the PeftModel and use its return value, which is the plain transformers model with merged weights; if you call it on the base model you get "AttributeError: 'Qwen3ForCausalLM' object has no attribute 'merge_and_unload'". safe_merge=True checks the merged weights for NaNs. The prompts use the same system prompt and the same empty think block as training, on 20 held-out rows. The gate is the argmax at every prompt position: bf16 re-rounds W plus B times A times alpha over r, with alpha 32 and rank 16, so a scale of 2; logits move by about 0.06, which is one bf16 rounding step for values near 10, but the top token must stay the same. Think of it as re-typesetting a contract: the font can shift a pixel, but every word must be the same. A likely question: why not assert exact equality? Because it fails on harmless rounding, and the deployment decision is the token the model picks. The merged folder is about 1.2 GB and loads without peft. This is the last step of the refunds lab: the model goes behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Option A serves the merged copy, which is right for one tenant, or for the GGUF path: GGUF is the llama.cpp file format for CPUs, laptops and phones. Option B keeps one bf16 base on the GPU and loads LoRA adapters by name. Here the shipping adapter stands for a second team's adapter, trained with the same recipe. vLLM defaults to max_loras 1 and max_lora_rank 16, so for two adapters we pass --max-loras 2. The VRAM bar is the real cost picture: vLLM takes 90% of the GPU by default; the weights are about 1.2 GB and two adapters about 80 MB, and the rest becomes KV cache for concurrent requests. Think of the base as a shared kitchen and each adapter as a recipe card. The client sends the same system prompt as training and enable_thinking false through chat_template_kwargs, so the prompt prefix matches what the model learned; without it you get garbage think text. A likely question: why does the adapter work in Python but not in vLLM? Under transformers v5 the module names can differ; compare logprobs of base and adapter in CI, and try --model-impl transformers (PEFT issue 3896). Next: before we leave Lab 1, how to port an old tutorial to this stack.
Gotcha TRL 1.16 / PEFT 0.21 / transformers 5.20

Port a pre-1.0 TRL tutorial: one loud error, then two silent defaults

old_tutorial.py · written for trl 0.x
# tok and ds as in Lab 1 steps 1-2
trainer = SFTTrainer("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", tokenizer=tok,
    args=SFTConfig(output_dir="out", max_seq_length=1024,
                   warmup_ratio=0.03),
    train_dataset=ds["train"],
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, task_type="CAUSAL_LM"))
SymptomTypeError: SFTTrainer.__init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'tokenizer' CauseTRL 1.x renamed the kwargs. SFTConfig also rejects max_seq_length and warmup_ratio. Fixprocessing_class, max_length, warmup_steps=0.03. Pin trl==1.16.0.
fixed.py · trl 1.16.0
trainer = SFTTrainer("Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", processing_class=tok,
    args=SFTConfig(output_dir="out", max_length=1024,
                   warmup_steps=0.03,              # float = ratio
                   model_init_kwargs={"dtype": torch.bfloat16}),
    train_dataset=ds["train"],
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
                           target_modules="all-linear"))
print(next(trainer.model.parameters()).dtype)   # torch.bfloat16
Most SFT tutorials on the web are pre-1.0, and porting one to TRL 1.16 fails in two ways. The loud way: tokenizer is now processing_class, max_seq_length is max_length, and warmup_ratio is gone in transformers v5, where warmup_steps takes a float below 1 as a ratio; each of these raises a TypeError, which is easy to fix. The silent way comes after the renames, when the run starts: with no target_modules, PEFT uses the qwen3 default of q_proj and v_proj only, so 2.29 million trainable parameters instead of 10.09 million with all-linear; and SFTTrainer loads a string model id in float32, so a 0.6B model takes about 2.4 GB of weights instead of 1.2 GB, before gradients and optimizer states. Both give a worse or more expensive run with no warning. Fix both as in Lab 1 step 2, and log the dtype at step 0. Think of it like a rental car with the seat set for somebody else: it drives, but not well, until you check every setting. A likely question: "Why does TRL keep float32 as the default?" The maintainers keep it on purpose because their training-inference mismatch results were measured at that precision. Next: the same refund rows on managed Gemini tuning, with no GPU of our own.
Build Acme refunds assistant · managed SFT on Vertex Gemini

Same refund data, no GPUs: managed SFT on gemini-3.5-flash

python vertex_sft.pygoogle-genai==2.33.0Docs Use supervised fine-tuningCodelab Fine-tune Gemini on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
refunds_sft/vertex_sft.py · same rows, split and SYSTEM as Lab 1
import os, time
from google import genai
from google.genai import types
from common import SYSTEM
from to_gemini_jsonl import upload_lab1_split  # Lab 1 split -> JSONL
BUCKET = os.environ["TUNING_BUCKET"]           # gs://my-project-tuning
upload_lab1_split(BUCKET)   # refund_train.jsonl, refund_val.jsonl in GCS
client = genai.Client(http_options=types.HttpOptions(api_version="v1beta1"))
job = client.tunings.tune(
    base_model="gemini-3.5-flash",
    training_dataset=types.TuningDataset(gcs_uri=f"{BUCKET}/refund_train.jsonl"),
    config=types.CreateTuningJobConfig(
        tuned_model_display_name="refund-agent-v1", epoch_count=3,
        validation_dataset=types.TuningValidationDataset(
            gcs_uri=f"{BUCKET}/refund_val.jsonl"),
        adapter_size=types.AdapterSize.ADAPTER_SIZE_FOUR))
while not job.has_ended:             # property: state in JOB_STATES_ENDED
    time.sleep(60)
    job = client.tunings.get(name=job.name)
resp = client.models.generate_content(model=job.tuned_model.endpoint,
    contents="I was charged twice for order {{Order Number}}, refund one",
    config=types.GenerateContentConfig(system_instruction=SYSTEM,
        thinking_config=types.ThinkingConfig(
            thinking_level=types.ThinkingLevel.MINIMAL)))
print(job.state, resp.text)

Open weights · Lab 1You own the GPU (Ampere+, ≥ 12 GB: L4, A10G, A100), the loss mask, the LoRA, the merge and serving.
Managed · this slideGoogle owns GPUs, training and serving. You get an endpoint. 0 GPUs no SLA
Limits: ≤ 131,072 tokens per example, ≤ 1 GB per JSONL file.
These are the same 2,992 refund rows, the same train and test split and the same system prompt as Lab 1, but now Google runs the training. Set up once: application-default login, enable the Vertex AI API, create a bucket in the us multi-region, and export the project, the location us, the enterprise flag and the bucket. Click 1: a small helper in the repo, to_gemini_jsonl.py, writes each Lab 1 row as one Gemini SFT line, with a systemInstruction and user and model parts, and copies the train and validation files to Cloud Storage. Click 2: client.tunings.tune on gemini-3.5-flash with adapter size four and three epochs; the adapter size sets how many adapter parameters train, like the LoRA rank, and Gemini 3.5 Flash allows 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16. Click 3: poll until the job ends. The location must be the us or eu multi-region, not us-central1, or the job fails. Then read tuning_data_stats: you pay for training tokens times epochs, so truncated or dropped examples cost money and quality at the same time. Click 4: call the tuned endpoint with the same system instruction as training and thinking level MINIMAL, because the model learned from data with no thinking. Think of it as sending laundry out instead of buying a washing machine: no hardware, but you accept their sizes, their queue and no guarantee. Two more gotchas: a raw string in training_dataset raises a pydantic ValidationError, and a second concurrent job hits the global quota of one. A likely question: "When should I pick the open-weights path?" When you need the weights, control of the loss mask, multi-LoRA serving or an SLA, which managed SFT does not give: it is not a Covered Service. Next: the third path, Gemma 4, where TRL masking breaks and Unsloth fixes it.

gemma4_router.py · router: request → {category, intent} JSON · REFUND → Lab 1
from unsloth import FastModel        # import unsloth FIRST: it patches trl
from unsloth.chat_templates import get_chat_template, train_on_responses_only
import json
from datasets import load_dataset
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer
model, tokenizer = FastModel.from_pretrained("unsloth/gemma-4-E2B-it",
    max_seq_length=1024, load_in_4bit=True)   # Unsloth kwarg, not SFTConfig
model = FastModel.get_peft_model(model, finetune_vision_layers=False,
    finetune_language_layers=True, finetune_attention_modules=True,
    finetune_mlp_modules=True, r=16, lora_alpha=16, lora_dropout=0)
tokenizer = get_chat_template(tokenizer, chat_template="gemma-4")
SYSTEM = "Classify the customer ticket. Reply with JSON only."
def to_text(r):
    label = json.dumps({"category": r["category"], "intent": r["intent"]})
    convo = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM},
             {"role": "user", "content": r["instruction"]},
             {"role": "assistant", "content": label}]
    return {"text": tokenizer.apply_chat_template(convo, tokenize=False)}
raw = load_dataset("bitext/Bitext-customer-support-llm-chatbot-training-dataset",
                   split="train").shuffle(seed=3407).select(range(6000))
trainer = SFTTrainer(model=model, processing_class=tokenizer,
    train_dataset=raw.map(to_text, remove_columns=raw.column_names),
    args=SFTConfig(dataset_text_field="text", max_steps=200, learning_rate=2e-4,
        per_device_train_batch_size=2, gradient_accumulation_steps=4))
trainer = train_on_responses_only(trainer,
    instruction_part="<|turn>user\n", response_part="<|turn>model\n")
trainer.train()
model.save_pretrained_gguf("gemma4-router-gguf", tokenizer, quantization_method="Q8_0")
Acme now wants a small router in front of the refunds assistant: it labels each request with category and intent as JSON over the 27 Bitext intents, on a free T4 with Gemma 4 E2B. A REFUND label sends the request to the Lab 1 adapter. Start on the left: the plain TRL path fails at once, because assistant_only_loss needs a training-compatible chat template, and TRL 1.16 patches Gemma and Gemma 3 but not Gemma 4. Click 1: Unsloth. Import unsloth first so it can patch trl and transformers. max_seq_length is Unsloth's own loader argument, not the TRL SFTConfig field we renamed earlier. With r=16 about 25 million of 5.1 billion total parameters train; E2B means about 2 billion effective parameters. The data map builds one text field per row with the gemma-4 template. Click 2: Gemma 4 uses turn markers that differ from Gemma 3, so old tutorial markers match nothing. Click 3: train_on_responses_only gives every user token the label minus 100, so only the JSON label trains. We pass instruction_part and response_part explicitly, because auto-detection can fail with "Could not auto-detect chat template structure - pass instruction_part and response_part." Think of the mask as a highlighter: the model reads the whole page but is graded only on the highlighted answer. Click 4: export a Q8_0 GGUF, one of the three formats Unsloth supports for Gemma 4 today, and probe three prompts with llama.cpp's llama-cli. Click 5: a GGUF export from a raw PeftModel wrapper silently ships the base model (unsloth issue 11698), so load the adapter with FastModel before export. Next: we have checkpoints from three paths; the last slide shows how to pick the one to ship.
arXiv Sep 2026

Pick SFT checkpoints by generated accuracy, not by validation loss

arXiv:2609.36569 29 Sep 2026

From Checkpoint Variation to Selection Gains in SFT

60 math SFT runs: generation-based picks (generated accuracy / checkpoint agreement) beat matched NLL picks by +0.71 / +0.85 percentage points (pp).
Score every checkpoint on ≥ 300 items with the task metric.
refunds_sft/step3b_score_checkpoints.py · after step 3
import glob, re, torch
from peft import PeftModel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
from common import refund_splits
BASE, PH = "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B", re.compile(r"\{\{[^}]+\}\}")
tok, test = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE), refund_splits()["test"]
for ck in sorted(glob.glob("qwen3-0.6b-refund-lora/checkpoint-*")):
    base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
    model, kept = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, ck).eval(), 0
    for r in test:
        enc = tok.apply_chat_template(r["messages"][:2],   # SYSTEM + user
            add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False,
            return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True)
        out = model.generate(**enc, max_new_tokens=128, do_sample=False)
        reply = tok.decode(out[0, enc["input_ids"].shape[1]:])
        gold = set(PH.findall(r["messages"][2]["content"]))
        kept += gold <= set(PH.findall(reply))
    print(ck, "placeholder_kept", round(kept / len(test), 3))

Post-Training Science for SFT: 4 customer datasets, Qwen3 and Llama up to 235B. Validation loss may not rank downstream quality.
Sweep the learning rate first, then rank the runs by the task metric.
The Lab 1 refund adapter saves one checkpoint per epoch, and we set load_best_model_at_end to False, so which one do we ship? The September paper on 60 math SFT runs compares two generation-based rules, generated accuracy and checkpoint agreement, with picking by validation NLL: they win by 0.71 and 0.85 percentage points. That sounds small, but it is free once you have the eval set, and a validation set of about 300 items instead of 32 adds about 0.3 more; the gain over simply keeping the final checkpoint stayed unresolved, so measure it on your task. The chart is a schematic: both rows start at zero, and the guide lines show that the lowest-loss checkpoint and the most accurate checkpoint are different columns. Click 2: the scoring script loads each checkpoint, generates greedily with the training prefix, and counts whether every placeholder of the gold reply survives. Click 3: our sweep shows the same trap: r64 has the lowest eval_loss but a worse intent score than r16, so we ship r16. Rank and learning rate change together in these three rows, which is why the second paper says: sweep the learning rate first, then compare ranks at a fixed rate. intent_exact runs the Gemma 4 router on each reply and compares its intent with the gold intent. Loss is like a typing-speed test for a lawyer: it is related to the job, but you hire on the case results.
03
QLoRA and honest before/after evaluation

QLoRA, then prove it

A 4B model fits a 16 GB GPU in NF4. The adapter counts only when the same weights score better with it on.

Qwen3-4B · NF4 · LoRA r=16
This chapter is Lab 2: the Acme claims desk wants free-text adjuster notes turned into strict JSON with four keys: loss_type, severity, needs_adjuster and policy_section. The picture shows the plan. The bf16 weights use 16 bits per weight, about 8.1 GB for 4.06 billion parameters. We load the same weights in 4-bit NF4, about 2.3 GB (not exactly a quarter, because some parts such as the quantization constants are extra), so the frozen base fits a 16 GB GPU. Beside it sits the LoRA adapter: a small folder with adapter_model.safetensors and adapter_config.json that loads on top of the base, and that we can switch on and off. Then comes the honest part: we score the same quantized weights twice, once with the adapter off and once with it on, so quantization noise is identical in both arms. Analogy: a clinical trial where the control group takes the same pill without the active ingredient. Likely question: "Why not compare against the bf16 base?" Because then you measure quantization and the adapter together, and you cannot tell which one moved the number.
Lab 2 Acme claims extractor · step 1 of 4

Prompt-completion rows mask the prompt for any chat template

python lab2_rows.pyCPU · secondsDocs TRL SFT Trainer
claims_sft/lab2_rows.py · datasets 5.1.0
# lab2_rows.py - gate the claims rows before any GPU time
import json, sys
from datasets import load_dataset
KEYS = {"loss_type", "severity", "needs_adjuster", "policy_section"}
ds = load_dataset("json", data_files={"train": "claims_train.jsonl",
                                      "validation": "claims_val.jsonl"})
print(list(ds), ds["train"].column_names)   # prompt, completion

def bad_row(r):                              # wrong keys or broken JSON
    try:
        return set(json.loads(r["completion"][0]["content"])) != KEYS
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return True

bad = [(s, i) for s in ds for i, r in enumerate(ds[s]) if bad_row(r)]
if bad:
    sys.exit(f"{len(bad)} bad rows, first: {bad[:5]}")
print("bad rows: 0")

One row has two columns. prompt holds the system and user turns. completion holds the JSON answer.
Prompt tokens get label -100, the ignore index of PyTorch cross-entropy. They add zero loss. TRL does this when both columns exist.
assistant_only_loss needs {% generation %} marks in the chat template. TRL adds them for Qwen3, not for Gemma 4. Prompt-completion rows need no marks.
The gate exits on a bad row, so no GPU time is lost. claims_test.jsonl never trains and never picks a checkpoint.
Lab 2 starts with the data, because the row format decides what the model learns. Each JSONL row has two columns: prompt, with the system and user turns, and completion, with the assistant's JSON answer. Export the three files from the claims system in this format; the test file has 200 rows and stays locked away for step 4. When both columns exist, TRL's completion_only_loss defaults to True, so every prompt token gets label -100, which is the ignore index of PyTorch cross-entropy, and only the JSON is in the loss. Note on the diagram: the words stay readable, they only stop counting. assistant_only_loss does the same job for conversational rows, but it needs generation marks in the chat template; TRL patches Qwen3, which is why Lab 1 can use it, but it does not patch Gemma 4, which then raises "The chat template is not training-compatible". Prompt-completion rows avoid that question for any model. Do not add a formatting_func: TRL raises "A formatting function was provided while completion_only_loss=True, which is incompatible." Analogy: an exam sheet where the question is printed and only the answer box is graded. Likely question: "What does the gate catch?" A completion with the wrong keys or broken JSON; sys.exit returns code 1, so a CI job stops before any GPU time.
Lab 2 Acme claims extractor · step 2 of 4

QLoRA in one trainer call: NF4, double quant, paged 8-bit Adam

lab3_qlora_claims.py · trl 1.16.0 · transformers 5.20.2 · bitsandbytes 0.50.2
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from transformers import BitsAndBytesConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer
DT = torch.bfloat16 if torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported() else torch.float16  # T4: fp16
PREC = {"bf16": DT == torch.bfloat16, "fp16": DT == torch.float16}   # SFTConfig flags
print("dtype:", DT)
ds = load_dataset("json", data_files={"train": "claims_train.jsonl",
                                      "validation": "claims_val.jsonl"})
bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",              # default is "fp4": always set nf4
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,         # quantize the quantization constants too
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=DT)
args = SFTConfig(
    output_dir="qwen3-4b-claims-qlora", model_init_kwargs={"dtype": DT},
    **PREC, max_length=1024, learning_rate=1e-4, num_train_epochs=3,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4, gradient_accumulation_steps=4,  # T4: batch 2
    optim="paged_adamw_8bit",               # QLoRA paged optimizer
    eval_strategy="epoch", save_strategy="epoch", logging_steps=10, report_to="none")
trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507", args=args,
    train_dataset=ds["train"], eval_dataset=ds["validation"],
    quantization_config=bnb,                # trainer argument only
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
                           target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM"))
trainer.model.print_trainable_parameters()  # step 3 checks this number
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("qwen3-4b-claims-qlora/final")
python lab3_qlora_claims.py nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used --format=csv -l 5
Set nf4 and double quant. BitsAndBytesConfig defaults to fp4; the TRL CLI defaults to nf4.
Pass quantization_config to SFTTrainer only. Setting it in model_init_kwargs too raises ValueError. TRL places the model on the GPU and sets the adapter dtype.
paged_adamw_8bit keeps 8-bit Adam states. It pages them to CPU RAM only when GPU memory runs out.
T4 has no bf16. DT and PREC switch the dtype, the compute dtype and the bf16/fp16 flags together.
output · illustrative · first line
dtype: torch.float16    # T4 · L4, A10G, A100: torch.bfloat16
This is the complete QLoRA script for the Acme claims extractor: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 in 4-bit, LoRA r=16 on all linear layers, and one SFTTrainer call. First band: set nf4 and double quant yourself, because BitsAndBytesConfig defaults to fp4 without double quant, while the TRL CLI defaults to nf4, so a script and a CLI run called "QLoRA" can differ. Second band: give quantization_config to the trainer only; TRL moves it into model_init_kwargs, so setting it there as well raises a ValueError, and TRL also places the model on the GPU and casts the adapter, so you need neither device_map nor prepare_model_for_kbit_training. Third band: the paged 8-bit Adam keeps small optimizer states; paging to CPU RAM happens only when a memory spike would otherwise cause an out-of-memory error, so at normal settings the states stay on the GPU. Fourth band: a T4 has no bf16, and SFTConfig defaults to bf16=True, so the DT line switches the model dtype, the compute dtype and the bf16/fp16 flags in one place; on a T4 also use batch size 2. Think of NF4 as a zip file of the weights that is decompressed one layer at a time for each matrix multiply. Likely question: "How long does it take?" Read train_runtime at the end of the log; it depends on the GPU and on the number of rows, so measure it on your data.

from transformers import AutoConfig
c = AutoConfig.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507")
r, h, ff = 16, c.hidden_size, c.intermediate_size   # r from lab3_qlora_claims.py
q, kv = c.num_attention_heads * c.head_dim, c.num_key_value_heads * c.head_dim
per_layer = r * ((h + q) + 2 * (h + kv) + (q + h)   # q, k, v, o
                 + 2 * (h + ff) + (ff + h))         # gate, up, down
print(per_layer, per_layer * c.num_hidden_layers)   # 36 layers

Loss is not the task metric. eval_loss averages over all completion tokens. A weak stop token barely moves it, so prose can still follow the JSON. Step 4 scores the JSON.
The first line of train.log is the one to check: 33,030,144 trainable parameters, about 0.8% of the 4.06 billion in Qwen3-4B. check_params.py recomputes that count from config.json, and the table shows the arithmetic: r times in plus out for q, k, v, o, gate, up and down gives 917,504 per layer, and 36 layers give 33,030,144. If your number is much smaller, target_modules did not match, and you know before you read any loss. The second panel is the head and tail of train.log, not output of check_params.py. The chart shows the first of three epochs: the loss falls from 0.902 to an eval_loss of 0.142; the run continues to epoch 3 and saves that adapter to final. But loss is not the business metric. eval_loss averages over every completion token, so one weak end-of-turn token hardly changes it, and the model can still write prose after the closing brace. Step 4 measures JSON validity on held-out notes. Think of the adapter as the steering wheel on a heavy truck: small, but it decides where the whole model goes. Likely question: "Why is QLoRA slower per step than LoRA?" Every forward pass dequantizes the NF4 weights. AQLoRA (arXiv 2608.23816, Aug 2026) keeps the layers with the highest NF4 error in fp16 and trains 11.3 ± 2.3% faster, at a cost of 0.1 to 1.5 accuracy points; its layer choice matches Unsloth's dynamic-4bit checkpoints.
Lab 2 Acme claims extractor · step 4 of 4

Same NF4 weights, adapter off vs on

lab4_eval_before_after.py · peft 0.21.2 · transformers 5.20.2
# omitted above: imports; tok; test = claims_test.jsonl (200 rows);
# base = Qwen3-4B in NF4 with the same bnb and DT as lab3_qlora_claims.py
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, ADAPTER).eval()
FIELDS = ["loss_type", "severity", "needs_adjuster", "policy_section"]
def generate(msgs):
    enc = tok.apply_chat_template(msgs, add_generation_prompt=True,
                                  return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True).to(model.device)
    with torch.no_grad():
        out = model.generate(**enc, max_new_tokens=96, do_sample=False)
    return tok.decode(out[0, enc["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)
def score():
    valid, hits = 0, dict.fromkeys(FIELDS, 0)
    for ex in test:
        gold = json.loads(ex["completion"][0]["content"])
        try:
            pred = json.loads(generate(ex["prompt"]))
        except json.JSONDecodeError:      # prose after the JSON: invalid
            continue
        if isinstance(pred, dict):
            valid += 1
            for f in FIELDS:
                hits[f] += pred.get(f) == gold[f]
    n = len(test)
    return {"json_valid": valid / n, **{f"acc_{f}": hits[f] / n for f in FIELDS}}
with model.disable_adapter():          # BEFORE: same weights, LoRA off
    before = score()
after = score()                        # AFTER: same weights, LoRA on
for k in before:
    print(f"{k:20s} base={before[k]:.3f} tuned={after[k]:.3f}"
          f" delta={after[k] - before[k]:+.3f}")

do_sample=False overrides Qwen's generation_config (sampling, temperature 0.7, top_p 0.8). Decode only the new tokens.
JSONDecodeError: Extra data on the base is expected: it adds prose. The row counts as invalid.
disable_adapter() runs the same NF4 weights with LoRA off. Quantization noise is the same in both arms.
Adapter on, same test set. The delta now isolates the adapter.
This is the honest test: one model object, the same 4-bit NF4 weights, and the adapter switched off for the "before" run with disable_adapter. Walk the code in order. First, generation is greedy: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 ships a generation_config that samples, with temperature 0.7 and top_p 0.8, so do_sample=False makes the metric reproducible, and we decode only the new tokens so the prompt never reaches json.loads. Second, a JSONDecodeError on the base model is expected, because it adds prose after the JSON, and that row counts as invalid. Third, disable_adapter gives the "before" scores on the same weights, so quantization noise is identical in both arms. Fourth, the "after" run gives the delta, and all four keys, including the free-text policy_section, are scored. The numbers are illustrative on 200 notes. With n=200 and a score near 0.6, the 95% interval is about plus or minus 0.07 (normal approximation), so a delta of 0.38 is far outside the noise; chapter 11 adds proper intervals and a slice table. Also run a general-capability regression on both arms, because forgetting is the main SFT cost; the forgetting slide (NB-LoRA) shows how large it can be. If the adapter fails to load with "Target modules ... not found in the base model", the adapter was trained on a different base: load the base named in adapter_config.json. Likely question: "Why not compare against the base loaded separately in bf16?" Because then you also measure quantization, and you cannot tell which change moved the score.
Gotcha QLoRA and export

QLoRA traps: fp4 by default, 4-bit merges drift, exports ship the base

1 · Quant type
SymptomA copied script scores below the recipe. CauseNo bnb_4bit_* lines: fp4, no double quant. FixOne bnb with nf4 for every loader.
2 · Merge into 4-bit Repo PEFT #3878
SymptomEach merge / unmerge cycle moves the base. CauseA merge into 4-bit quantizes again: lossy. FixA/B on a reloaded base. Merge into bf16.
3 · GGUF export Repo Unsloth #11698
SymptomThe GGUF answers exactly like the base. CauseA PeftModel wrapper makes the export skip the merge. FixLoad the adapter folder with FastModel.
qlora_fixes.py · transformers 5.20.2 · peft 0.21.2 · unsloth 2026.10.8 (pip install "unsloth==2026.10.8")
from unsloth import FastModel   # first import: Unsloth patches transformers
import torch
from peft import PeftModel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig
BASE, ADAPTER = "Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507", "qwen3-4b-claims-qlora/final"
# 1 · one bnb for every loader (lab3 training, lab4 eval): nf4 + double quant
bnb = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
                         bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16)
base4 = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE, quantization_config=bnb)   # A/B: reload, never merge
# 2 · export: merge into a fresh bf16 base, then compare greedy outputs on 50 rows
base16 = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
merged = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base16, ADAPTER).merge_and_unload(safe_merge=True)
merged.save_pretrained("qwen3-4b-claims-merged")
# 3 · GGUF: load the adapter folder through Unsloth in 16-bit, export, then run 3 probes
model, tokenizer = FastModel.from_pretrained(model_name=ADAPTER, load_in_4bit=False)
model.save_pretrained_gguf("claims-gguf", tokenizer, quantization_method="Q8_0")
Three traps cost QLoRA teams days, and none of them raises an error. Trap one: BitsAndBytesConfig without the bnb_4bit lines falls back to fp4 with no double quantization, while the TRL CLI defaults to nf4, so a script and a CLI run both called QLoRA are different runs. Lab 2 sets both explicitly; reuse one bnb object in every script that loads the base. Trap two: PEFT warns "Merge lora module to 4-bit linear may get different generations due to rounding errors". Merging into 4-bit weights quantizes them again, so merge then unmerge does not give the base back, and each cycle drifts further. Reload the base for A/B tests, merge into a bf16 copy for export, and check that greedy outputs of the merged model match the adapter model on 50 held-out rows. Trap three: an Unsloth GGUF export through a PeftModel wrapper silently ships the base model, because the export method is bound to the base object. Load the adapter folder with FastModel; with load_in_4bit=False the merge happens in 16-bit, not in 4-bit. Then run three probe prompts on the GGUF: the answers must differ from the base. Unsloth pins its own transformers range, so install it in a separate environment. A related report: a merged Gemma 4 gave garbled output while the adapter-only save worked (Unsloth #7318); gate each merge by comparing perplexity of merged and adapter models on 50 rows, within about 1%. Think of a 4-bit merge like photocopying a photocopy: every pass loses a little.
Gotcha PEFT target modules · peft 0.21.2

DPO loss pinned at ln 2: LoRA reached only 4 of 56 layers

SymptomDPO-LoRA on NVIDIA-Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2: 25 of 25 steps finish, loss 0.6931 on every step. CausePEFT's default targets for nemotron_h are attention only: 4 of 56 layers. PEFT raises only when no target matches (#3658, open). FixTarget all-linear. Assert per-layer coverage before training.
DPO loss = −log σ(β·Δ). Δ = 0 (policy = reference) gives ln 2 = 0.6931.
check_lora.py · cfg
cfg = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, task_type="CAUSAL_LM")   # default targets
check_lora.py · cfg
cfg = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
                 target_modules="all-linear")   # + Mamba and MLP projections
check_lora.py · peft 0.21.2 · transformers 5.20.2
import torch
from peft import LoraConfig, get_peft_model
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2",
                                             dtype=torch.bfloat16)
m = get_peft_model(model, cfg)                # cfg from the box above
hit = {n.split(".lora_A")[0] for n, _ in m.named_parameters() if "lora_A" in n}
layers = {int(n.split("layers.")[1].split(".")[0]) for n in hit if "layers." in n}
assert len(layers) == model.config.num_hidden_layers, \
    f"LoRA on {len(layers)} layers only"

Count the layers that have a lora_A. 4 != 56 stops the run before the first training step.
Lab 2 model: PEFT's default for qwen3 is q_proj, v_proj only. Lab 2 sets all-linear; keep the assert in CI.
Lab 2 was safe because we passed all-linear; this trap appears when the default targets meet a hybrid model. The bug report: a DPO-LoRA run on NVIDIA-Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 finished 25 of 25 steps, nothing crashed, and the DPO loss sat at 0.6931 on every step. Quick DPO reminder: the loss is minus log sigmoid of beta times the margin between the policy and the reference; when the policy equals the reference the margin is zero, and the loss is ln 2. So the adapter barely changed the model. The cause: this model has 56 layers, 27 Mamba-2, 25 MLP and only 4 attention, and PEFT's default targets for nemotron_h are attention projections. PEFT raises only when nothing matches, so a partial match is silent. Partial coverage does not always pin the loss exactly at ln 2; here the 4 attention layers were too small a share of the model to move it in 25 steps. The fix: target all-linear, which adds the Mamba in_proj and out_proj and the MLP up and down projections, and assert one LoRA layer per decoder layer before training. For the Lab 2 model the same lesson holds: PEFT's default for qwen3 is q_proj and v_proj only, which on Qwen3-0.6B gives 2.3 million instead of 10.1 million trainable parameters. A related load-time trap: PEFT drops unexpected adapter keys without a warning, and strict=True is ignored (PEFT #3804), so diff the adapter keys against the model keys and check that the adapter answer differs from the disable_adapter answer on 5 notes. Think of a dimmer switch wired to 4 bulbs out of 56: the switch moves, the room stays dark.
arXiv Jul–Sep 2026 · three papers

SFT on a reasoning model can erase its reasoning: constrain the update

arXiv:2609.25618 22 Sep 2026

Reasoning-Preserving Fine-Tuning of Post-RL LLMs with Null-Basis LoRA

Plain LoRA SFT drops reasoning 63.8% → 8.3% (Qwen2.5-3B) and 80.1% → 9.4% (1.5B). NB-LoRA trains ΔW = B·C·NsT in the null space of reasoning activations: same task accuracy, reasoning near pre-FT, 6.3x faster than NSCL.
When you SFT a thinking model like Qwen3, re-run a reasoning benchmark on both arms.
arXiv:2607.23711 26 Jul 2026

The Intruder Threshold: A Spectral Law for LoRA Fine-Tuning

Predicts which LoRA layers grow forgetting-driving intruder dimensions. Mistral-7B r256: forgetting +4.71 → +1.77 WikiText-2 PPL. A uniform lower alpha, or half the LR, works about as well.
If you see forgetting, lower alpha or LR first.
arXiv:2607.21351 23 Jul 2026

How Much Can a LoRA Adapter Memorize?

LoRA stores 2–3.4 bits per parameter. At equal accuracy, SFT memorizes ~3x more example-specific information than GRPO.
Add a general-capability regression to lab4_eval_before_after.py.
arXiv 2609.25618 arXiv 2607.23711 arXiv 2607.21351
Chapter 3 fine-tunes a Qwen3 model, so ask what the update damages, not only what it teaches. NB-LoRA shows the risk on post-RL models: plain LoRA SFT took reasoning from 63.8% to 8.3% on Qwen2.5-3B, because the update overlaps the directions the reasoning activations use. The fix collects about 512 reasoning rollouts, takes the null space of each layer's inputs, and trains the update only there, so the reasoning inputs see no change; picture painting a wall with tape over the window. The Intruder Threshold paper adds the cheap lesson: if you see forgetting, a lower alpha or half the learning rate works about as well as its per-layer rule. A likely question is whether this matters for privacy: the memorization paper finds SFT stores about 3x more example-specific information than GRPO at equal accuracy, so keep a general-capability regression in the before/after script.
Best practices

Ten SFT rules that each prevent a failure we saw in code

  • Pin versions; pass dtype.The float32 default doubles memory.
  • Prove the mask in CI.Fail on sum(mask)==0 or no stop token.
  • target_modules="all-linear"Qwen3/Llama/Gemma3 default: q, v only.
  • LR 1e-4 to 2e-4; set alpha.Three tools, three defaults (below).
  • QLoRA: nf4; merge into bf16.Default is fp4; 4-bit merges drift.
  • Select checkpoints on the task.Beats NLL by 0.71-0.85 pp; gate on adapter on/off.
  • Do not SFT new facts.Hallucination rises (2608.30987); use RAG.
  • Same think block in train and serve.Vertex: thinking_level MINIMAL.
  • Serve with multi-LoRA.Merge only for GGUF or edge.
  • Managed: check the limits.us/eu, 5,000 val cap, no SLA.
assistant_only_loss: loss on replies only. Lab 1 proves it.
all-linear, and set alpha: the defaults differ by tool.
warmup_steps: 0.03 is a ratio. warmup_ratio raises TypeError in v5.

Each rule on this slide maps to a bug we hit in the labs, so read it as a pre-flight list, not as theory. The first five protect the training run: pin the stack, prove the mask in CI, target all linear layers, set alpha yourself, and use nf4 explicitly because the transformers default is fp4. The next five protect the release: pick checkpoints on the task metric, keep facts in RAG, keep one think-block convention, serve adapters with multi-LoRA, and read the managed-tuning limits. The table is the reason for rule four: TRL CLI, PEFT and Unsloth ship different alpha defaults, so "r=16" gives an update scale of 2.0, 0.5 or 1.0 depending on the tool. Think of it like a recipe that says "one cup" when three kitchens use three cup sizes. A likely question: "Why not just pick the lowest eval loss?" Answer: the lowest-loss checkpoint is often not the best task score, which is why Lab 2 gates on the adapter off/on delta, and 2609.36569 shows generation-based selection beats NLL selection.
04

Rewards you can unit-test

A reward function is code. Test it with a known hack before it meets a GPU.

Acme refunds desk: refund-decision agent gold labels from the policy engine one reward: TRL 1.16.0 · OpenAI graders · Vertex Gemini RFT unit tests: Python 3.11+, CPU, no packages Docs TRL GRPO Trainer
This chapter is Lab 3: the Acme refunds desk has an agent that answers with an answer block holding decision, refund_amount and reason, and the policy engine of record gives the gold labels. We write the reward once as plain Python, unit-test it on a CPU with hand-written completions, and then run the same logic in TRL GRPO, as an OpenAI python grader, and as a Vertex Gemini RFT reward. Watch the loop: the good answer scores 1.0, but the hack and the broken answer must score 0.0, and only then does the CI check go green. Analogy: you test a smoke detector with test smoke before you trust it to guard the building. Likely question: "Why test a reward at all, it is ten lines?" Because our first draft of this exact reward paid 0.5 to a schema-less hack, and GRPO amplifies any cheap partial credit it finds.

GRPO scores answers against their group, so cheap partial credit wins

GRPO samples 8 completions per prompt. Advantage = (r − group mean) / group std, scale_rewards="group".

A 0.5 that costs zero tokens beats a 0.0 in its group. Gate partial credit on validity.

gate: not REQUIRED <= obj.keys() → 0.0

All 8 equal: advantage 0, no gradient. TRL logs it as frac_reward_zero_std.

Repo TRL v1.16.0 grpo_config.py arXiv 2610.21404 Multi-Reward Hacking (TAG) Repo TRL v1.16.0 grpo_trainer.py
GRPO has no value model: it samples 8 completions for one refund prompt, scores them, and each completion's advantage is its reward minus the group mean, divided by the group standard deviation; that is scale_rewards="group", the TRL 1.16 default. Step through it: two correct answers get big green arrows, the zeros get small red ones, and the hack in card 3, which scored 0.5 under our first draft without any amount or reason, sits above the mean of 0.31, so GRPO pushes the policy toward it. With the schema gate it scores 0.0 and its arrow turns red. In the last step every rollout scores 0.0, the standard deviation is 0, so all advantages are 0 and that prompt gives no gradient at all; TRL counts it in frac_reward_zero_std. Analogy: a teacher who grades on a curve rewards whatever beats the class average, even a blank page with the right heading. Likely question: "Then is partial credit bad?" No, graded credit gives variance when nobody is fully right, but it must be gated on a valid answer, as arXiv 2610.21404 shows for multi-reward GRPO. Next, Lab 3 writes this gated reward in code.
Lab 3 Acme refund-decision agent · step 1 of 4

Two refund rewards in TRL's signature: format and gated decision

refunds_rl/refund_rewards.py · trl 1.16.0 reward contract
import json, re
ANSWER_RE = re.compile(r"<answer>\s*(\{.*?\})\s*</answer>", re.DOTALL)
DECISIONS = {"approve", "deny", "escalate"}
REQUIRED = {"decision", "refund_amount", "reason"}

def _parse(text):  # the JSON dict inside <answer>...</answer>, or None
    m = ANSWER_RE.search(text)
    try:
        obj = json.loads(m.group(1)) if m else None
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return None
    return obj if isinstance(obj, dict) else None

def format_reward(completions, **kwargs):  # 0.2 = parses, 3 keys, valid decision
    out = []
    for c in completions:
        obj = _parse(c[0]["content"])
        ok = obj is not None and REQUIRED <= obj.keys() and obj.get("decision") in DECISIONS
        out.append(0.2 if ok else 0.0)
    return out

def decision_reward(completions, gold_decision, gold_amount, **kwargs):
    out = []  # 1.0 decision + amount within $0.01 | 0.5 decision only | 0.0 otherwise
    for c, gd, ga in zip(completions, gold_decision, gold_amount, strict=True):
        if gd is None:  # no gold label: TRL skips this reward for the row
            out.append(None)
            continue
        obj = _parse(c[0]["content"])
        if obj is None or not REQUIRED <= obj.keys() or obj.get("decision") != gd:
            out.append(0.0)
            continue
        try:
            amount_ok = abs(float(obj.get("refund_amount")) - float(ga)) <= 0.01
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            amount_ok = False
        out.append(1.0 if amount_ok else 0.5)
    return out

Schema gate: no partial credit unless all 3 keys exist.
None becomes NaN, so TRL skips this reward for the row. strict=True stops silent misalignment.
Lab 3 starts here and runs four slides: write the reward, test it, then port it to OpenAI graders and to Vertex Gemini RFT. This is the reward for the Acme refund-decision agent, written in the exact signature that TRL 1.16.0 GRPOTrainer calls, and it runs on a laptop CPU with no packages. Step 1: format_reward reads the text from c[0]["content"] because completions are message lists, and the **kwargs catch-all is required because TRL also passes prompts, completion_ids, trainer_state, log_extra, log_metric and every dataset column. Step 2: decision_reward asks for gold_decision and gold_amount by name, and TRL fills them from the dataset columns with the same names, so there is no glue code. Step 3: the schema gate means no partial credit unless all three keys are present; step 4: returning None for a row without a gold label tells TRL to skip this reward for that row, and zip with strict=True turns a silent misalignment into an error. Analogy: the reward is an exam marker who must refuse to mark a paper that is not on the official answer sheet. Likely question: "Why not just return 0.0 for unlabelled rows?" Because 0.0 is a real score that pushes the policy down, while None removes the row from this reward entirely. Next, step 2 runs the self-test and shows the hack it caught.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    good = ('<think>Item unopened, 12 days.</think><answer>{"decision": "approve", '
            '"refund_amount": 49.99, "reason": "within 30 days"}</answer>')
    wrong_amt = '<answer>{"decision": "approve", "refund_amount": 40, "reason": "x"}</answer>'
    hack = '<answer>{"decision": "approve"}</answer> approve deny escalate'
    broken = "Sure! I approved it."
    comps = [[{"role": "assistant", "content": t}]
             for t in (good, wrong_amt, hack, broken)]
    print("format  :", format_reward(comps))
    print("decision:", decision_reward(comps, gold_decision=["approve"] * 4,
                                       gold_amount=[49.99] * 4))
    print("no-label:", decision_reward(comps[:1], gold_decision=[None], gold_amount=[None]))

Now we run the file. It needs no GPU and no packages, and it finishes in seconds. Steps 1 to 4: four hand-written completions go through both rewards; the good answer gets 0.2 and 1.0, the wrong amount gets 0.2 and 0.5, and the hack and the broken answer get 0.0 and 0.0, which is the exact output on the CPU. Step 5 is why this test exists: our first draft had no REQUIRED gate, and the hack that only says approve and then lists every decision earned 0.5, and inside a GRPO group a free 0.5 beats a 0.0, so the policy would learn it. Step 6: test TRL's own built-ins the same way; think_format_reward wants the completion to start with a think tag, and the soft overlong penalty is a linear ramp from 384 to 512 tokens. Analogy: a known hack in the test suite is like a fire drill, you prove the alarm rings before the real fire. Likely question: "How many hack cases are enough?" Start with at least one per reward, for example right key with no answer, keyword stuffing, empty JSON and the answer in the wrong tag, and add each new hack you find in training logs. Same logic as an OpenAI multi-grader: test locally, validate, run

pip install "openai==3.37.0"export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...python openai_grader.py
refunds_rl/openai_grader.py · openai 3.37.0 · same 0 / 0.5 / 1 logic
from openai import OpenAI
GRADE_SRC = r'''
import json, re
def grade(sample, item) -> float:
    m = re.search(r"\{.*\}", sample["output_text"], re.DOTALL)
    if not m:
        return 0.0
    try:
        out = json.loads(m.group(0))
    except Exception:
        return 0.0
    if not {"decision", "refund_amount", "reason"} <= out.keys(): return 0.0  # schema gate
    if out.get("decision") != item["gold_decision"]:
        return 0.0
    try:
        ok = abs(float(out.get("refund_amount", -1)) - float(item["gold_amount"])) <= 0.01
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        ok = False
    return 1.0 if ok else 0.5
'''
policy = {"type": "python", "name": "policy", "source": GRADE_SRC}
tag = {"type": "string_check", "name": "tag", "operation": "ilike",   # must cite the policy id
       "input": "{{sample.output_text}}", "reference": "{{item.policy_id}}"}
grader = {"type": "multi", "name": "refund_grader", "graders": {"policy": policy, "tag": tag},
          "calculate_output": "0.8 * policy + 0.2 * tag"}
item = {"gold_decision": "approve", "gold_amount": "49.99", "policy_id": "RP-30"}
sample = ('<answer>{"decision": "approve", "refund_amount": 49.99, '
          '"reason": "Unopened, day 12 of 30 (RP-30)"}</answer>')
ns = {}
exec(GRADE_SRC, ns)                                  # 1) free local unit test first
print("local policy score:", ns["grade"]({"output_text": sample}, item))
client = OpenAI()                                    # 2) server-side checks
print(client.fine_tuning.alpha.graders.validate(grader=grader))
run = client.fine_tuning.alpha.graders.run(grader=grader, model_sample=sample, item=item)
print("reward:", run.reward, "sub:", run.sub_rewards, "errors:", run.metadata.errors)

Step 3 of Lab 3 ports the refund reward from step 1 to an OpenAI python grader: grade(sample, item) keeps the same schema gate, so it returns 0 for unparseable output, a missing key or a wrong decision, 0.5 for the right decision with the wrong amount, and 1.0 when both match. A string_check grader adds 0.2 for citing the policy id, and the multi grader combines them with the formula 0.8 * policy + 0.2 * tag, where the formula names must match the graders keys. Always exec the source locally first: it is free, and the step 2 completions give 1.0 for good, 0.5 for wrong_amt, 0.0 for the hack, the broken answer and a deny. Without the gate line the hack scores 0.5 here too, so port the gate with the logic. Then validate and run it on the server; a sample that passes both sub-graders must print 1.0, which checks the formula. The LAUNCH_RFT block that calls jobs.create on o4-mini-2025-04-16 is omitted, because o4-mini shut down on 2026-10-23 and OpenAI is winding down fine-tuning; think of the grader as a recipe you can cook in any kitchen. Next, step 4 cooks the same recipe on Vertex Gemini RFT. A likely question: "Why not fetch the policy from our API inside the grader?" Because python graders have no network, so import requests fails and every sample scores 0.
